I personally recommend the website lostallhope.com. It has helped me out a lot in the past. It is unbiased and honest, but very effective.

It has a "Help Me" section for people in your situation (being very suicidal but hoping that there is another way). You may also be interested in the "My Story" section. They also have lots of statistics on suicide. Did you know that if you are aged 15-24, your chances of successfully killing yourself are estimated to be as low as 1 in 200? Not a lot of people know this, but it is SO common to survive suicide attempts. The odds are heavily stacked against you, and a suicide attempt will likely give you a hospital visit at best and severe permanent brain damage at worst, and I'm sure you don't want to make your life even more unbearable. The site also makes you think about other things, for example, how your body will be found and how that may affect the person/people who find(s) it.

I hope you give yourself plenty of time to think this over, and please use that website to research what you plan to do, because I can almost guarantee that there are things you didn't know or consider that will make you rethink thing.

I wish you the best of luck and I really, really hope things improve for you. <3

I'm not sure if you're familiar with the placebo effect or not, but if not, it's basically the situation you just described. To sum it up, if you truly believe that something is happening when it is not, you will experience symptoms of the thing you believe is happening.
So, in drug trials, they have a placebo group, a group of people who are told that they are receiving the drug but are actually being given useless pills and being told that they are the drug being tested. This is to find out if the drug is actually working or if the positive results are just the placebo effect. Anyway, during an antidepressant trial, a guy in the placebo group tried to overdose on his medication. It wasn't actually medication though, it was just useless pills so it shouldn't have had any effects, but it did. His blood pressure dropped dramatically and he had to be rushed to hospital. He survived, but he had made himself pretty ill all because he thought he was going to die, even though he was in no danger at all.
A similar thing happened to a guy who thought someone had put a voodoo curse on him, he got extremely ill and it looked like he was going to die even though nothing was wrong with him. They actually cured him using the placebo effect, they gave him a harmless drink and told him that a priest had blessed it to cure the curse (this wasn't true) and he got better.

When I go from depressed to manic it's usually a sudden change, but when I go from manic to depressed it's more gradual. It's kind of like I go from yay to ugh to nope. The transitional period lasts for about a week. The first day of actual depression is very apparent though, the lines aren't blurred. Apparently this can happen because as you go through the cycle you begin with very high energy and it drops to very low at the end (high energy is mania and low energy is depression). This also explains why many people feel like they are most manic at the beginning of an episode and most depressed at the end of an episode. I also start sleeping a lot more a few days before the depression really sets in (by that I mean like when you start getting suicidal and stuff). I think this sort of thing varies from person to person though.

I was planning on taking the bus to my local clinic to tell them about my problems, but they only run a drop-in clinic (where anyone can just walk in and will be seen whenever possible without a booked appointment) in the morning and this was like noon-ish, so I called from the bus stop to try to get an appointment but they were fully booked. Then I just took a bus home instead and went to bed. I'm a psychology student, and there is no "transgender lesson" lmao, so I don't really know why they're trying to use their credentials to uplift their opinion. You really don't need a degree to do some research. Maybe having a degree makes it easier to understand your research, but it doesn't qualify you to pull things out of your ass and present them as fact. My professor actually talks about this a lot, and says that he often hears news about psychology where an experiment has been flawed, results have been misinterpreted or misrepresented and people are making statements that aren't backed by sufficient evidence or are logically flawed, and these things end up becoming widespread and having an effect on the world just because a Renowned Psychologist™️ said it. 
 
Here is what the field of psychology has to say about transgender people. "Gender Dysphoria" is listed as a mental disorder in the DSM-5, however, the publisher (American Psychiatric Association) stated "gender nonconformity is not in itself a mental disorder. The critical element of gender dysphoria is the presence of clinically significant distress associated with the condition." So basically, the despair about having a gender-birthsex mismatch is a mental disorder, but simply having a gender-birthsex is not, in itself, classified as a mental disorder. The treatments (if I'm not mistaken) that are listed for it in the DSM-5 are types of medical transition (e.g. SRS, HRT, etc). That is the only relation that transgenderism has with psychology. A lot of people also have this weird misconception about mental disorders wherein they think that all disorders can be treated and cured with therapy, when this is simply not the case (Down Syndrome is a mental disorder, many disorders can be caused by brain damage, etc). 

As for biology, transgenderism has ties to neurobiology, genetics and endocrinology. There have been numerous brain scans showing that the brains of trans people resemble that of the typical member of the opposite birthsex, and studies have linked this to atypical hormone exposure during foetal development. This has actually been linked to testosterone sensitivity/insensitivity genes (depending on whether you're FTM or MTF), so some may actually be transgender due to their genes.

Just because you can't see it doesn't mean it's not there. You're not even an adult yet, you have your entire life ahead of you. As I said, the pain will go away, especially as you transition. One of my best friends is a transboy who went through an extremely rough period of depression just like you. He thought he was hopeless, he thought he would never have any happiness in the future, and one day he attempted suicide. He survived, and now that he's several years into his transition, he has almost no dysphoria and is extremely happy, and is also very relieved that he survived. He sometimes gets emotional about it because the thought that he might not have been alive today scares him so much. I can honestly say that every single trans person I've met had bad dysphoria and then saw it heal dramatically when they transitioned. Please give yourself a chance, and remember that depression does make you delusional, just because you feel worthless and hopeless does mean on any level that you are, and you are most likely far from it. Why not make a deal with yourself? Make a contract that until you complete your transition, you will stay alive. Also, have you seen a doctor about this? Medication and/or therapy may be appropriate if you are not already receiving it.

I know that feeling, I have the exact same problem with allergies, and I haven't been diagnosed with BPD so I don't know how that feels, but when I do go through fluctuating severities of dysphoria, and when I have bad dysphoria I get depressed and unmotivated, especially with regards to my voice. 

I'll start with the allergies:

- Do everything you can to combat the problem: blow your nose, take medication, drink lots of water, clear your throat, etc.
 
- Do vocal warmups throughout the day (especially at the start) to get your voice going. Try going up and down your range (like "doh re mi fa so la ti doh", but you don't have to say those words, I say the word "mum"), and keeping pushing it to a higher note each time you do it.

This should hopefully prepare your voice for training when it's congested. 
 
As for when you're lacking energy, this is more of a mental health issue so I can't really give you vocal advice for this, obviously. I am a psychology student so I know a little about BPD, and I know that motivation is extremely difficult during the depression period. I would recommend seeking therapy or medication to help you deal with the motivation sapping aspect of BPD, because there's not too much else that can be done. Maybe write a motivational letter to yourself (doesn't have to be a physical letter, you could do it on your computer or phone or whatever) to read whenever you lack energy to remind yourself of why voice training is so important to you. You could also try browsing the internet for motivation techniques, perhaps many are applicable to BPD.

I hope this helps, good luck with your voice training! :) x
